# Brief: design SNOBOL4's storage runtime over PL/SW primitives

**Owner:** dcsno
**Branch:** `pr/storage-allocation-runtime`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
**Prerequisite:** read
`/disk1/.../work/dcpls/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-plsw/docs/storage-allocation.md`
first. That doc describes the PL/SW substrate this saga builds
on. **This brief is design-and-plan only — the PL/SW
`?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` macros do not exist yet.** Mike will
signal when dcpls's `pr/storage-macros` saga has shipped and
`plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` is available for linking.

You can read this brief now, audit your existing allocation
sites, and draft a runtime design. Don't push the migration
commit until prerequisites are confirmed live.

## Context

SNOBOL4 on PL/SW has a high-frequency allocation pattern:
parsing source, building pattern objects, evaluating matches,
backtracking, building strings. Today the SNOBOL4 source under
`sw-cor24-snobol4/src/` either doesn't allocate (uses static
buffers) or rolls a bump arena ad hoc. As `compiler.sno` and
larger programs land, this stops scaling.

The PL/SW design doc lays out a clean layering:

> PL/SW provides only the raw alloc/free primitives. Region
> boundaries, mark/reclaim, and garbage collection live in the
> consumer's runtime.

That means `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` will give SNOBOL4 a
free-list-backed `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(n), ADDRESS(p), RC(rc))` and
`?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(p), LENGTH(n), RC(rc))`. **Anything beyond
those two primitives — region save/restore, mark/sweep,
generational GC, per-context heaps — is yours.**

Why this split: Prolog wants WAM-style trail unwinding, future
Fortran wants common-block static + stack frames, future C-like
guests want plain malloc/free. Each has its own storage policy
on top of the same dumb substrate. SNOBOL4's policy lives in
SNOBOL4's runtime.

## Goal

After this saga: SNOBOL4 has a documented, implemented storage
runtime that scales to the workloads it'll see (`compiler.sno`,
pattern-heavy demos, etc.). The runtime calls `?GETMAIN` /
`?FREEMAIN` (or the underlying `_PLSW_GETMAIN`/`_PLSW_FREEMAIN`
procedures) as primitives and adds whatever policy SNOBOL4
needs on top.

## Two reasonable designs to choose from

Both are valid. Pick the one that fits SNOBOL4's actual
allocation profile; this brief is not prescriptive about which.

### Design A: GC over a single big region

- One `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(BIG))` at startup carves out the whole
  SNOBOL4 heap (e.g. 32 KB or 64 KB).
- SNOBOL4's runtime owns that region: cell allocator, mark/sweep
  (or copying) GC, root-set traversal of the SNOBOL4 stack /
  variable table, etc. PL/SW's free-list is never touched after
  startup; `?FREEMAIN` is called once at program exit (or never).
- Pros: traditional SNOBOL4 model, no per-cell PL/SW call
  overhead, full control over headers and tags, handles arbitrary
  liveness graphs.
- Cons: more code (a real GC). Need a precise root set, which
  means cooperating with PL/SW's calling convention to find live
  cells in stack frames and registers.

### Design B: region-stack over `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN`

- Multiple `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(REGION_SIZE))` blocks form a stack
  of regions (think arena-per-pattern-match-attempt).
- Each match attempt pushes a region; on backtrack, the region
  is `?FREEMAIN`'d wholesale.
- Long-lived data (symbol table, compiled patterns) lives in a
  base region that's never popped.
- Pros: simpler than full GC; matches SNOBOL4's natural
  pattern-match scope structure; fragmentation is bounded
  because each region is freed wholesale.
- Cons: cells that escape a region (e.g. captured by an outer
  match) need explicit promotion to an older region or
  copy-out. Cells that don't escape are free; cells that do
  cost the copy.

A third hybrid (small fixed-size cell pool for high-churn
allocations, region-stack for variable-size work, GC only over
the symbol table) is also possible. Whichever approach you take,
**the doc-of-record for "what is SNOBOL4's storage model" lives
in `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/`**, not in PL/SW.

## What this saga delivers

Pick one of these scopes; both are reasonable as standalone
sagas:

- **Scope A: Design + plan only.** Audit current allocation
  sites, write `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/storage.md` describing
  the chosen runtime model (A, B, or hybrid), draft an interface
  for the runtime procedures (e.g. `_SNO_ALLOC_CELL`,
  `_SNO_GC_COLLECT`), but don't implement yet. Implementation is
  a follow-up saga.
- **Scope B: Design + minimum runtime.** Same docs as Scope A
  plus an MVP of the chosen runtime — enough to handle
  `examples/hello.sno` and one pattern-matching demo without
  static buffers. Subsequent sagas widen coverage.

Pick whichever fits your bandwidth. If unsure, do Scope A first
— design errors here are cheap to fix on paper, expensive to fix
in shipped runtime code.

## Migration mapping (when ready)

For Scope B (or for whenever the runtime lands), each existing
allocation site moves from `DCL ... BYTE; DCL ... INT INIT(0);`
ad-hoc bump arenas to either:

```pl/i
?GETMAIN(LENGTH(N), ADDRESS(P), RC(RC));
/* ... use P ... */
?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(P), LENGTH(N), RC(RC));
```

… or a SNOBOL4-runtime call that wraps `?GETMAIN` with policy:

```pl/i
P = SNO_ALLOC_CELL(KIND_STRING, length);
/* ... use P ... */
/* GC reclaims when no longer reachable */
```

Inventory your existing call sites with:
```sh
grep -nE 'ARENA_POS|arena_alloc|ALLOC.*PROC' sw-cor24-snobol4/src/
```

## What goes in this PR (Scope A version)

1. Audit of existing allocation sites in `src/`.
2. `docs/storage.md` describing the chosen runtime model.
3. Drafted interface for `_SNO_ALLOC_*` (or whatever names fit)
   procedures.
4. Plan for which allocation sites move first when the runtime
   ships.
5. Optional: a sample `.plsw` showing the call shape, against a
   stub `_PLSW_GETMAIN` that returns 0 (so the design is at
   least syntactically validated against PL/SW today).

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` source — that's dcpls's saga
  (`pr/storage-macros`). Don't implement the substrate; depend
  on it.
- No PL/SW compiler or macro changes.
- No SNOBOL4 language changes (no `.sno` source rewrites).
- No allocation runtime that conflicts with the eventual
  PL/SW substrate (e.g. don't reimplement `?GETMAIN`'s job in
  SNOBOL4 source — call it).

## When done

Push `pr/storage-allocation-runtime` and signal mike. Promotion
to `dev`/`main` is mike's call. After dcpls's `pr/storage-macros`
ships, SNOBOL4's runtime can land in a follow-up saga (or this
saga's Scope B can be extended in place if not yet relayed).

## Questions to answer in your design doc

1. What is the dominant allocation size in SNOBOL4? (Tiny cells?
   Medium strings? Variable patterns?) The answer should drive
   the choice between Design A (GC over big region) and Design B
   (region-stack).
2. What is the rooted set during pattern matching? (i.e. which
   pointers must remain valid across a `?GETMAIN`?) If you can't
   enumerate this concisely, GC is harder; region-stack may be a
   better fit.
3. Are there any natural "scope boundaries" in SNOBOL4 execution
   where you could drop everything cheaply? (Match attempt?
   Statement boundary? Function call?) Region-stack maps cleanly
   onto these.
4. Worst-case live set — how big can the SNOBOL4 heap get before
   you'd consider it pathological? That sets the reasonable
   default for `PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` in your `%INCLUDE plsw_storage`
   line.

content.text:
Yes, four:

**1. Path/filename: `include/storage.msw`?** The existing shared .msw files live there (`cvt.msw`, `ascb.msw` etc. — though those are data-structure headers; `storage.msw` would be the first runtime/library .msw). Or do you want it elsewhere (a new `runtime/`, or top-level)?

**2. Default heap size when `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` isn't set?** Design doc didn't pin a number. Reasonable defaults: 4096 (cautious; SNOBOL4 will override anyway), 8192 (one quarter of usable SRAM ish, leaves headroom for code+stack), 16384 (generous; matches the bumped p24p source buffer size). I'd lean 8192 for the default; the consumer overrides per-program.

**3. Procedure names — `_PLSW_GETMAIN` / `_PLSW_FREEMAIN`?** Per the design doc and the existing `__plsw_div` namespacing convention. Or shorter (`_GETMAIN` / `_FREEMAIN`)?

**4. Scope of this saga:** macros + implementation only, OR also (a) `examples/storage_demo.plsw` + reg-rs golden case `plsw_storage_demo`, and/or (b) some kind of self-test for alloc/free/coalesce/OOM/double-free? The brief I drafted listed those tests as deliverables for `pr/storage-macros`; they're real coverage but they're meaningful work too. Acceptable answers: "macros only — tests in a follow-up", "macros + demo only", or "macros + demo + full reg-rs coverage in this saga."

Minor ones I'll just decide unless you push back:
- 6-byte block header (3-byte size, 3-byte next-when-free pointer, naturally aligned to COR24's 3-byte word).
- First-fit, coalesce-on-free with the immediately-following neighbor (no backward coalesce — adds a doubly-linked-list cost we don't need for SNOBOL4's pattern).
- `SUBPOOL` clause silently ignored if passed (forward-compat with the design doc's "reserved for future multi-arena").
- `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(0))` → return success with address 0 (rather than OOM); cheaper than a real allocation, callers can check for null.
- Headers stored *inside* the heap region (not in a separate side table) so the heap is self-describing.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about GETMAIN and FREEMAIN syntax in z/OS:

## GETMAIN/FREEMAIN Syntax Overview

In z/OS assembler programming, the GETMAIN and FREEMAIN macros have one positional parameter called the "form" of the macro.

### GETMAIN Syntax

The standard syntax for GETMAIN includes the **LV** parameter for specifying length. From the search results, here's an example from actual z/OS code:

GETMAIN RU,LV=(5),LOC=(24,ANY)

Where:
- **RU** - The form (Register Update)
- **LV=(register)** - Specifies the length using a register
- **LOC=(24,ANY)** - Specifies storage location constraints

### FREEMAIN Syntax

Similarly, FREEMAIN RU,LV=(0),A=(11) shows the corresponding FREEMAIN syntax where:
- **RU** - The form
- **LV=(register)** - The length of storage being freed
- **A=(register)** - The address of the storage to be freed

The key difference is that in z/OS GETMAIN/FREEMAIN macros, **LV** requires a register specification (indicated by parentheses), rather than being a direct parameter name like in CICS command-level statements.

content.text:
## IBM FREEMAIN history

**Yes, FREEMAIN required explicit length on OS/MVS through z/OS.** All variants (R, E, RU, VRU, VU) take `LV=length` as a required parameter. The classic spelling:

```
FREEMAIN RU,LV=DATALEN,A=(R1),SP=SP000
```

The historical reason: the OS/360-lineage allocator didn't keep an in-band header on every block (in the early forms it used the GQE/FQE chains stored *outside* the user region). Callers had to remember the length they GETMAIN'd. CICS FREEMAIN later relaxed this because CICS tracked allocations itself.

This means we have a real design choice for `?FREEMAIN`:

- **(a) Modern (header-only):** `?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(p), RC(rc))` — drop LENGTH. Recover size from the in-band header. Diverges from IBM PL/X spelling but matches `free(p)` ergonomics.
- **(b) Faithful (length-required):** `?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(p), LENGTH(n), RC(rc))` — require LENGTH per IBM. Use header as source of truth; cross-check the passed length against it; mismatch sets non-zero RC. Honors PL/X aesthetic and gives a free corruption check.
- **(c) Faithful but lenient:** require LENGTH in the macro signature for spelling continuity, but ignore it (header wins). Worst of both worlds.

I'd lean **(b)** — you wanted PL/X spelling aesthetics, and the cross-check catches both header corruption and "caller passed wrong length" (a real bug class). The cost is one comparison.

## Other answers you settled

1. **Two-file pattern**: `include/storage.msw` (macros + `EXTERNAL` decls) + `lib/storage.plsw` (new `lib/` dir; `%DEFINE LIBRARY` impl + heap region). Consumer does both `%INCLUDE storage;` *and* adds `storage` to their meta-gen + link24 modules list. No automatic link-when-include — it's documented convention. (Or do you want `lib/` somewhere else, like reusing `examples/` or making a `runtime/`?)
2. **Default heap**: 65536 bytes. Override via `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE NNNNN;` before `%INCLUDE storage;`.
3. **Names**: `_PLSW_GETMAIN`, `_PLSW_FREEMAIN`, `_PLSW_HEAP_BUF`, `_PLSW_FREE_HEAD`, `_PLSW_INITIALIZED`. All `_PLSW_` prefixed.
4. **Scope**: macros + impl + demos + reg-rs goldens. Concrete reg-rs cases I'm planning: `plsw_storage_basic` (alloc/use/free, RC=0), `plsw_storage_coalesce` (alloc A B C, free B then A → free list shows one big block), `plsw_storage_oom` (alloc until RC≠0), `plsw_storage_double_free` (free same address twice → RC≠0 on second), `plsw_storage_size_mismatch` (only if you pick option (b) above — pass wrong LENGTH to ?FREEMAIN, expect RC≠0). Each gets an `examples/storage_*.plsw` driver.

## Drops

7. SUBPOOL: gone, no clause.
8. LENGTH(0): gone, no special case — caller can check before calling, or get whatever the allocator does naturally (probably allocates a 6-byte header for a 0-byte body, returns valid address; `?FREEMAIN` of it works normally).

## Three small new questions

A. **Lazy init or explicit `?STORAGE_INIT;`?** Lazy: first `?GETMAIN` checks `_PLSW_INITIALIZED`, sets up the single-block free list. Explicit: caller must invoke once. Lazy is cleaner; explicit is more debuggable. I'd default to lazy.

B. **Allocation alignment**: 3-byte (COR24 word) alignment for both headers and bodies, so `la` loads stay aligned. OK to bake in?

C. **Where does `lib/storage.plsw` go?** Three options:
- New `lib/` dir — clean separation but adds a new convention.
- `runtime/storage.plsw` — matches the "PL/SW runtime library" framing.
- `src/storage.plsw` alongside the compiler source — wrong, it's not compiler source.

I'd pick `lib/` unless you want `runtime/`.

Sources:
- [IBM Documentation — FREEMAIN macro](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zvm/7.2.0?topic=macros-freemain)
- [GETMAIN / FREEMAIN versus STORAGE OBTAIN / STORAGE RELEASE — IBM Mainframes](https://ibmmainframes.com/about65700.html)
- [OS/390 GETMAIN/FREEMAIN — SAS Documentation](https://support.sas.com/documentation/onlinedoc/sasc/doc700/html/lr2/zwritget.htm)
- [IBM Mainframe Assembler — Macros (Les Smith)](http://www.les-smith.com/software/assembler/macros.htm)

content.text:
We have a linker — it's the `link24` + `meta-gen` pair that landed in your `pr/bootstrap-toolchain` saga, both now on PATH. SNOBOL4 already uses them. Let me walk the actual chain so the decision is grounded.

## What's already in place

- **`pl-sw`** (on PATH) — runs the PL/SW compiler. Compiles a single `.plsw` (with whatever `.msw` includes are registered via the FILE:/SOURCE: protocol) to a `.s`.
- **`cor24-asm`** — assembles `.s` → `.bin`/`.lgo`/`.lst`. Supports `--base-addr` (post your `pr/cor24-asm-base-addr` saga) for relocating module emission.
- **`meta-gen`** — two modes: `prep` (rewrite external `la rN, _LABEL` to placeholders + emit `.syms`); `emit` (read pass-1 `.lst` + `.syms`, produce `.meta` with EXPORT + FIXUP records).
- **`link24`** — combines multiple module `.bin`s + `.meta`s into one executable, applying FIXUPs to resolve cross-module references.

So PL/SW separate compilation is a ~9-step pipeline (compile each module, prep, pass-1 assemble, emit metadata, layout, pass-2 assemble with `--base-addr`, link). It works. `components/linker/tests/demo-plsw-modular.sh` exercises the whole thing end-to-end and passes today (`PASS: got 'HI'` — verified during the goldens bootstrap).

## What SNOBOL4 already does

`dcsno/sw-cor24-snobol4/scripts/build-modular.sh`:

```bash
ENTRY=sno_main
LIBS="sno_util sno_lex sno_exec"
ALL_MODULES="$ENTRY $LIBS"
```

For each module, it:
1. Compiles `src/$MOD.plsw` via `scripts/build.sh` (which runs the PL/SW compiler) → `build/mod/${MOD}.s`.
2. `meta-gen prep` → external refs become placeholders.
3. `cor24-asm` pass-1 (will be — currently `cor24-run --assemble`, but will switch when SNOBOL4 does its `pr/bootstrap-toolchain` migration).
4. `meta-gen emit` → `.meta`.
5. Computes `BASES` from sizes.
6. `cor24-asm --base-addr` pass-2 → `.bin`s with internal refs resolved.
7. `link24 --entry main --dir … --map …` → `build/snobol4.bin`.

**Adding storage to this is one line:** `LIBS="sno_util sno_lex sno_exec storage"`. The build loop picks it up like any other module. The compiled `_PLSW_GETMAIN` / `_PLSW_FREEMAIN` lands once in the final image; every module that calls them resolves via FIXUP.

So: not just-a-list-of-files-concatenated, but it's also not a heavy ceremony for SNOBOL4 — the ceremony is *already paid* by their existing build script. Storage is a free rider on infrastructure that's already there.

## The fork in the road

The real question is for **non-SNOBOL4 callers** — small `.plsw` programs (the `examples/storage_*.plsw` reg-rs cases I'm planning) that currently use the simple single-file pipeline (`pl-sw foo.plsw > foo.s; cor24-asm foo.s -o foo.lgo; cor24-emu --lgo foo.lgo`) and have never touched `link24` or `meta-gen`.

Two ways to give them `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN`:

**Path M (modular):** runtime ships as `runtime/storage.plsw` + `include/storage.msw`. Small programs that want a heap have to adopt the multi-step pipeline (meta-gen prep → pass-1 → emit → layout → pass-2 → link). My reg-rs cases would need a per-case driver that runs that full chain. Doable — we can put it behind a `scripts/build-modular-demo.sh` wrapper modeled on SNOBOL4's. But it complicates the small-program story.

**Path I (inline):** runtime ships as a single `include/storage.msw` containing the macros, the `_PLSW_GETMAIN` / `_PLSW_FREEMAIN` procedures, and the `DCL _PLSW_HEAP_BUF(PLSW_HEAP_SIZE) BYTE;` declaration. `%INCLUDE storage;` text-concats the whole thing into the program — exactly the path SNOBOL4 *would* take if they didn't already have a modular build. SNOBOL4 still works: they can either `%INCLUDE storage;` from `sno_main.plsw` (text-concat into entry module) or convert it to a `runtime/storage.plsw` library module and add to their LIBS — both yield the same final `.bin`. Small programs use the simple single-file pipeline unchanged.

**Path I cost**: each `%INCLUDE storage;` user gets a fresh ~150 lines compiled into their image. Not shareable across separately-compiled modules in the same image — if program X has two modules and *both* include storage, both end up with their own `_PLSW_GETMAIN`. With link24, that's a duplicate-symbol error. So Path I works cleanly only when the heap is included exactly *once* in the entry module.

**Path M cost**: simple programs have to learn the modular build. Less duplication; one allocator across the whole image.

## Recommendation

**Path I (inline, single `include/storage.msw`).** Your original instinct.

Reasoning:
- SNOBOL4 includes it from `sno_main.plsw` only (the entry module). Their other modules don't need to know about storage's internals — they just see `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` macros via their own `%INCLUDE storage;` *after* declaring `%DEFINE PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY;` (a guard the file checks via `%IF` to skip emitting the impl in non-entry modules). That avoids duplicate-symbol errors at link time.
- Small reg-rs demos (`storage_basic`, `storage_oom`, etc.) keep the existing single-file pipeline. No new build infrastructure for the test harness.
- The "where does the impl live" debate evaporates — it's in `include/storage.msw`. No new dir, no `runtime/`, no `lib/`.
- If a future program is so allocation-heavy that the per-translation-unit duplication matters, *then* extract to a separate `runtime/storage.plsw` module. Not yet.

Concrete shape for `include/storage.msw`:

```pl/i
/* Macros (always emitted) */
?GETMAIN MACRODEF; … END;
?FREEMAIN MACRODEF; … END;

%IF NOT DEFINED(PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY) THEN;
    /* Impl + heap (entry module only) */
    %IF NOT DEFINED(PLSW_HEAP_SIZE) THEN;
        %DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE 65536;
    %ENDIF;
    DCL _PLSW_HEAP_BUF(PLSW_HEAP_SIZE) BYTE;
    DCL _PLSW_FREE_HEAD INT INIT(0);  /* lazy-init sentinel */
    _PLSW_GETMAIN: PROC(SIZE INT) RETURNS(INT); … END;
    _PLSW_FREEMAIN: PROC(ADDR INT, LEN INT) RETURNS(INT); … END;
%ENDIF;
```

SNOBOL4's `sno_main.plsw` does `%INCLUDE storage;` once. The other SNOBOL4 modules either don't reference storage, or if they need the macros, they do `%DEFINE PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY 1;` then `%INCLUDE storage;` to get just the macro defs without re-declaring the heap.

Does that fit? If yes I'll start the saga that way. If you'd rather force the modular path even for tiny demos (Path M), say so and I'll write the demo runner.

# PL/SW Storage Macros Saga

Implements `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` and the underlying free-list
allocator per the design in `docs/storage-allocation.md`.
Single-file inline pattern (`include/_plsw_storage.msw`) so that
`%INCLUDE _plsw_storage;` text-concats macros + impl + heap into
the entry module. Multi-module consumers (SNOBOL4) use the
`PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY` guard to include only the macros in
non-entry modules. The `_plsw_` filename prefix reserves
`storage.{msw,plsw}` for application use (e.g., SNOBOL4's own
mark/reclaim runtime).

## Goal

After this saga: `%INCLUDE _plsw_storage;` brings `?GETMAIN` /
`?FREEMAIN` macros and the `_PLSW_GETMAIN` / `_PLSW_FREEMAIN`
procedures into a PL/SW program, plus a 64 KB default heap
(overridable via `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE`). The reg-rs test
suite covers basic alloc/free, coalesce-on-free, OOM, double-free
detection, and size-mismatch detection.

## Steps

1. **storage-macros**. Single step:
   - Implement `include/_plsw_storage.msw`: `%DEFINE
     PLSW_HEAP_SIZE 65536` default; `_PLSW_HEAP_BUF` byte array;
     `_PLSW_FREE_HEAD` and init flag; `_PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE)` and
     `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(ADDR, LEN)` procedures with first-fit
     allocation, forward-coalesce on free, and double-free
     detection via `next == 0xFFFFFF` allocated-magic; MACRODEFs
     for `?GETMAIN` and `?FREEMAIN` thin-wrapping the procs.
   - `PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY` guard so non-entry modules can
     get only the macros + EXTERNAL decls.
   - Add demos: `examples/storage_basic.plsw`,
     `storage_coalesce.plsw`, `storage_oom.plsw`,
     `storage_double_free.plsw`, `storage_size_mismatch.plsw`.
   - Wire each into `tests/driver.sh` and
     `scripts/bootstrap-goldens.sh`.
   - Bootstrap reg-rs goldens for the 5 new cases; verify
     `just test` passes 15/15 (the existing 10 + new 5).
   - Update `docs/storage-allocation.md` to reflect the
     implementation choice (single-file inline + headers-only
     guard) and note implementation details (coalesce policy,
     magic value for double-free detection, lazy init).

## Rules

- No PL/SW compiler logic changes.
- No SUBPOOL clause (per design doc; never needed for COR24).
- No backward-coalesce in v1 (documented as future).
- Free-list backend only (no bump/slab alternates).

`%INCLUDE _plsw_storage;` text-concats macros + impl + heap into
the entry module. Multi-module consumers (SNOBOL4) use the
`PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY` guard to include only the macros in
non-entry modules. The `_plsw_` filename prefix reserves
`storage.{msw,plsw}` for application use (e.g., SNOBOL4's own
mark/reclaim runtime).

(overridable via `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE`). The reg-rs test
suite covers basic alloc/free, coalesce-on-free, OOM, double-free
detection, and size-mismatch detection.

# PL/SW Compiler -- Usage Guide & Language Reference

## Building the Compiler

The PL/SW compiler is written in C and compiled by tc24r to run
on the COR24 emulator.

```bash
just build    # tc24r src/main.c -o build/plsw.s
```

## Compiling PL/SW Programs

Use the pipeline scripts to compile and run .plsw programs:

```bash
# Simple program (no includes)
just pipeline examples/hello.plsw

# Program with .msw include files (FILE: protocol)
just pipeline-dump include/cvt.msw include/ascb.msw examples/chain.plsw

# Shortcut targets for demos
just chain          # control block chain with .msw includes
just hello-macro    # macro invocation demo
```

### Pipeline Output

`pipeline-dump` produces three files in `build/`:

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `build/<name>.s` | Generated assembly with source line comments |
| `build/<name>-dump.txt` | Emulator memory dump (registers, SRAM, I/O) |
| `build/<name>-combined.plsw` | All .msw + .plsw concatenated with path comments |

## Source File Types

| Extension | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `.plsw` | PL/SW source code |
| `.msw` | Macro definitions and shared declarations |
| `.s` | Generated COR24 assembly (compiler output) |

## Compiler Modes

The compiler runs on the COR24 emulator with UART I/O. At startup
it prompts for a mode:

- **Suite number** (0-34) -- run a specific test suite
- **`a`** -- run all test suites
- **`c`** -- compile mode (accepts source via UART)
- **`r`** -- REPL (tokenizer)

### Compile Mode Protocol

In compile mode, the compiler accepts two input formats:

**Legacy** (single file): raw PL/SW source terminated by EOT (0x04).

**FILE:/SOURCE:** (multi-file): named include files followed by main source:
```
FILE:cvt.msw\n<content>\x1E
FILE:ascb.msw\n<content>\x1E
SOURCE:\n<main.plsw source>\x04
```

Each FILE: block registers content via `inc_register()` for `%INCLUDE` resolution.

## Language Reference

### Types

| Type | Width | Description |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `INT` or `INT(24)` | 3 bytes | Default 24-bit integer |
| `INT(16)` | 2 bytes | 16-bit integer |
| `INT(8)` | 1 byte | 8-bit integer |
| `BYTE` | 1 byte | Unsigned byte |
| `CHAR` | 1 byte | Character |
| `PTR` | 3 bytes | 24-bit pointer |
| `WORD` | 3 bytes | 24-bit unsigned |
| `BIT` | 1 byte | Boolean |

### Declarations

```plsw
/* Scalar */
DCL COUNT INT;
DCL FLAGS BYTE;
DCL LETTER CHAR;

/* With explicit width */
DCL ASID INT(16);

/* Array */
DCL BUFFER(80) CHAR;
DCL TABLE(10) INT;

/* String initialized (single or double quotes) */
DCL MSG(20) CHAR INIT('Hello from PL/SW!');
DCL CMD(24) CHAR INIT("OUTPUT = 'hello'");   /* single quotes inside double */
DCL APO(12) CHAR INIT('It''s fine');          /* doubled delimiter = literal */

/* Numeric initialized */
DCL ARENA_POS INT INIT(0);

/* Record with levels (1, 3, 5, ...) */
DCL 1 POINT,
    3 X INT,
    3 Y INT;

/* BASED record (template for pointer access) */
DCL 1 CVT BASED,
    3 CVTEYE(4) CHAR,
    3 CVTASCBH  PTR;

/* Pointer associated with preceding BASED record */
DCL CVTPTR PTR;

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/bootstrap-goldens.sh -- (re)create reg-rs golden files
# from the current toolchain's output.
#
# Run this once when first creating the golden baseline, or
# manually after an intentional behavior change lands. After
# bootstrap, commit the resulting reg-rs/plsw_*.{rgt,out,err}
# triples to git -- reg-rs compares stdout to .out, stderr to
# .err, and exit code to the value in .rgt. The .tdb files are
# reg-rs's internal SQLite index, regenerated from the triples
# at run time, and are gitignored.
#
# Prerequisites:
#   * `just build-lgo` produces build/plsw.lgo (currently blocked
#     on dcxtc/pr/array-size-expressions and
#     dcxtc/pr/string-literal-concatenation; see docs/testing.md).
#   * cor24-asm and cor24-emu on PATH.
#   * reg-rs on PATH.
#
# Each test is created via `reg-rs create -t plsw_<case> -c
# 'tests/driver.sh <case>'`. The command is run, its stdout +
# stderr + exit code captured, and a .rgt + .out pair written.

set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/.." && pwd)"
cd "$repo"

export REG_RS_DATA_DIR="$repo/reg-rs"

cases=(
    hello
    led
    loop
    record
    define
    select_demo
    select_nested
    macro
    hello_macro
    chain
)

# Ensure the compiler .lgo exists before we start. Without it the
# pipeline.sh inside driver.sh would re-trigger a tc24r build per
# case, which is wasteful and obscures real failures.
if [ ! -f "$repo/build/plsw.lgo" ]; then
    echo "bootstrap-goldens: building build/plsw.lgo first..." >&2
    just build-lgo
fi

for c in "${cases[@]}"; do
    echo "=== bootstrap: plsw_${c} ===" >&2
    reg-rs create -t "plsw_${c}" -c "./tests/driver.sh ${c}"
done

echo >&2
echo "Bootstrapped ${#cases[@]} golden(s) under reg-rs/. Commit:" >&2
echo "  git add reg-rs/plsw_*.rgt reg-rs/plsw_*.out reg-rs/plsw_*.err" >&2

## Macro contract

Two macros, both keyword-argument, modeled on the PL/X spelling:

```pl/i
?GETMAIN(LENGTH(expr), ADDRESS(lvalue), RC(lvalue));
?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(expr), LENGTH(expr), RC(lvalue));
```

| Clause | Required? | Type | Semantics |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LENGTH(expr)` | required for both | INT (bytes) | size of the block to allocate / free |
| `ADDRESS(...)` | required for both | PTR | `?GETMAIN` writes the allocated address to its lvalue; `?FREEMAIN` reads the address to free |
| `RC(lvalue)` | optional | INT | return code: 0 = success, non-zero = failure (out of memory on `?GETMAIN`; double-free / invalid pointer on `?FREEMAIN`). If omitted, the macro silently ignores failures. |
| `SUBPOOL(expr)` | reserved | INT | not in v1; reserved for a future multi-arena extension |

Expansion target: a normal procedure call sequence. The COR24
ISA has no SVC-equivalent instruction, so `?GETMAIN` expands to
something like:

```
push    LENGTH                ; arg
jal     r1, _PLSW_GETMAIN     ; r0 = address (or 0 on OOM)
sw      r0, ADDRESS           ; store result
ceq     r0, z                 ; rc = (r0 == 0) ? 1 : 0
…
```

(Exact expansion is an implementation concern; the contract is
"after `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(n), ADDRESS(p), RC(rc))`, `p` holds an
n-byte block on success or undefined on failure, and `rc` is 0
on success or non-zero on failure.")

Identical pattern for `?FREEMAIN`. Both run in O(1) caller-side
(one push, one call, one store); the allocator's complexity is
inside `_PLSW_GETMAIN`/`_PLSW_FREEMAIN`.
input.new_string:
## Procedure contract (v1)

Two procedures, called as ordinary PL/SW functions:

```pl/i
P  = _PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE);
RC = _PLSW_FREEMAIN(P, LEN);
```

| Procedure | Args | Return |
|---|---|---|
| `_PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE INT) RETURNS(INT)` | `SIZE`: bytes of user data wanted | address of user block (after the 6-byte header), or `0` on out-of-memory |
| `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(USERADDR INT, LEN INT) RETURNS(INT)` | `USERADDR`: address from `_PLSW_GETMAIN`. `LEN`: same size that was requested. | `0` on success; `1` on double-free / invalid pointer / corrupted header; `2` on size mismatch (`LEN` doesn't match the recorded size) |

`LEN` is required on free, mirroring IBM OS/MVS / OS/390
FREEMAIN. The implementation cross-checks `LEN` against the size
stored in the in-band header — mismatch returns `RC=2`. (See
"IBM heritage" note below for context.)

`SIZE=0` allocates a 6-byte block (header only, zero user data);
the returned address is valid and `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(addr, 0)`
frees it. No special case.

## Macro layer (deferred)

The PL/X-style spelling

```pl/i
?GETMAIN(LENGTH(expr), ADDRESS(lvalue), RC(lvalue));
?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(expr), LENGTH(expr), RC(lvalue));
```

is **not implemented in v1.** PL/SW's `MACRODEF`/`GEN DO` system
emits assembly directly — it does not expand to PL/SW source —
and `GEN` substitution is textual rather than AST-aware. That
makes it impossible to synthesize the right code for
arbitrary-expression `LENGTH` (literal works, runtime variable
doesn't) or arbitrary-lvalue `ADDRESS` (global label works,
stack-frame local doesn't).

For now, callers use the procedures directly. A future saga can
add `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` once PL/SW's macro system supports
AST-level expansion (or AT MINIMUM once it can emit a procedure
call to a runtime symbol with a typed expression argument). The
intended spelling above is the contract that future macro layer
will implement.

## Two-file opt-in pattern

PL/SW separate-compilation already supports the pattern via
`%DEFINE LIBRARY` modules linked through `meta-gen` + `link24`.
Storage uses the same shape:

```
plsw_storage.msw          declares ?GETMAIN/?FREEMAIN macros + EXTERNAL
                          decls of _PLSW_GETMAIN, _PLSW_FREEMAIN

plsw_storage.plsw         %DEFINE LIBRARY: provides _PLSW_GETMAIN,
                          _PLSW_FREEMAIN, and the heap region itself.
                          Heap size is configurable via %DEFINE
                          PLSW_HEAP_SIZE before %INCLUDE.
```

A consumer opts in by:

1. `%INCLUDE plsw_storage;` in their `.msw` (or directly in their
   `.plsw` if they don't have a header layer).
2. Adding `plsw_storage` to their link line (the modules list
   passed to `meta-gen` + `link24`).
3. Optionally declaring the heap size before include:
   ```pl/i
   %DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE 16384;
   %INCLUDE plsw_storage;
   ```

A program that doesn't `%INCLUDE plsw_storage` and doesn't link
in `plsw_storage.plsw` pays nothing — no heap region, no
allocator code, no impact on `.lgo` size. Opt-in is the contract,
not a build-time flag.
input.new_string:
## Single-file opt-in pattern

PL/SW v1 ships storage as a single inline `.msw`:

```
include/_plsw_storage.msw     macros (deferred), procedures, and
                              heap region. %INCLUDE'ing this file
                              text-concats everything into the
                              entry module.
```

The leading underscore in the filename (`_plsw_`) reserves
`storage.{msw,plsw}` for application use — SNOBOL4 can ship a
`runtime/storage.plsw` for its own mark/reclaim layer without
clashing.

A consumer opts in by:

1. (optional) Choose a heap size:
   ```pl/i
   %DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE 16384;     /* default 65536 */
   ```
2. Include the runtime in the entry module:
   ```pl/i
   %INCLUDE _plsw_storage;
   ```
3. (multi-module builds only) For non-entry modules that need to
   *call* `_PLSW_GETMAIN` / `_PLSW_FREEMAIN` but should not emit
   their own copy of the impl + heap, set the headers-only guard
   before include:
   ```pl/i
   %DEFINE PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY 1;
   %INCLUDE _plsw_storage;
   ```
4. Pass `include/_plsw_storage.msw` on the pipeline command line
   (the `FILE:` protocol registers it for `%INCLUDE` resolution):
   ```sh
   ./scripts/pipeline.sh include/_plsw_storage.msw your_program.plsw
   ```

A program that doesn't `%INCLUDE _plsw_storage` pays nothing —
no heap region, no allocator code, no impact on `.lgo` size.
Opt-in is the contract, not a build-time flag.

### Why single-file inline (and not modular .msw + .plsw)

The original design considered a two-file pattern
(`storage.msw` + `storage.plsw` linked via `meta-gen` + `link24`).
That remains a viable layout for downstream consumers (SNOBOL4
already builds modular), but for the PL/SW runtime itself the
single-file inline form is simpler:

- Tiny demos (the reg-rs golden cases) stay on the simple
  single-file pipeline. No modular build for two-line tests.
- SNOBOL4 already pays the modular-build tax; adding storage as
  a `%INCLUDE _plsw_storage;` in `sno_main.plsw` (only) is one
  line. Other SNOBOL4 modules use the `PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY`
  guard.
- A future "promote storage to a separate library module" saga
  is a non-breaking change — the `?GETMAIN` / `?FREEMAIN`
  contract stays the same, only the build steps change.

## Backend: free-list with embedded headers

PL/SW's `_PLSW_GETMAIN` is a **free-list allocator** with
embedded per-block metadata. This is the lowest-common-denominator
backend that supports both alloc and free with constant-time-ish
behavior:

- The heap region (`PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` bytes) is divided into
  variable-length blocks. Each block has a small header
  (~6 bytes: a `size` and a `next` pointer when free).
- Initially the heap is one giant free block.
- `_PLSW_GETMAIN(n)` walks the free list (first-fit), splits the
  chosen block into "allocated `n+header` bytes" and "remainder
  back on the free list," and returns the address past the
  header. Returns 0 if no block fits.
- `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(addr, n)` reads the block's header to find
  size, links it back into the free list, and coalesces with
  the next neighbor if it's also free.

## Backend: free-list with embedded headers

PL/SW's `_PLSW_GETMAIN` is a **free-list allocator** with
embedded per-block metadata. This is the lowest-common-denominator
backend that supports both alloc and free with constant-time-ish
behavior:

- The heap region (`PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` bytes, default 65536) lives
  in `_PLSW_HEAP_BUF[]`, a `BYTE` array declared at module scope.
- Each block has a 6-byte header at its start: 3-byte
  `BLOCK_SIZE` (total block size including header) followed by
  3-byte `BLOCK_NEXT` (when free: address of the next free block,
  or `0`; when allocated: `0xFFFFFF`, the alloc-magic sentinel).
- Free list is singly-linked, sorted by address ascending,
  pointed to by `_PLSW_FREE_HEAD`.
- Lazy init: first call to `_PLSW_GETMAIN` sets up one giant
  free block covering the entire heap. The `_PLSW_INIT_DONE`
  flag avoids re-init on subsequent calls.
- `_PLSW_GETMAIN(n)` walks the free list (first-fit), splits the
  chosen block into "allocated `n+6` bytes" and "remainder back
  on the free list" (only when the remainder leaves room for a
  useful block: `>= header + 1 byte`). Stamps the chosen block's
  `BLOCK_NEXT` with the alloc-magic sentinel. Returns the
  user-data address (block start + 6) or `0` on out-of-memory.
- `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(addr, n)` validates the alloc-magic sentinel
  (catches double-free + invalid-pointer), validates `n` matches
  the recorded block size (catches caller bookkeeping bugs),
  then sorted-inserts into the free list and forward-coalesces
  with the immediate-next free block if their address ranges
  abut.

**Forward coalesce only.** Backward coalesce (merge with the
immediate-previous free block) is deferred. Without it, a
sequence of allocations followed by frees in *forward order*
leaves N separate free blocks; freeing in *reverse order*
chain-coalesces them all. This is fine for SNOBOL4's expected
allocation pattern (LIFO-ish per pattern-match attempt) but
worth revisiting if profiling shows it matters.

- The heap region (`PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` bytes, default 65536) lives
  in `_PLSW_HEAP_BUF[]`, a `BYTE` array declared at module scope.
- Each block has a 6-byte header at its start: 3-byte
  `BLOCK_SIZE` (total block size including header) followed by
  3-byte `BLOCK_NEXT` (when free: address of the next free block,
  or `0`; when allocated: `0xFFFFFF`, the alloc-magic sentinel).
- Free list is singly-linked, sorted by address ascending,
  pointed to by `_PLSW_FREE_HEAD`.
- Lazy init: first call to `_PLSW_GETMAIN` sets up one giant
  free block covering the entire heap. The `_PLSW_INIT_DONE`
  flag avoids re-init on subsequent calls.
- `_PLSW_GETMAIN(n)` walks the free list (first-fit), splits the
  chosen block into "allocated `n+6` bytes" and "remainder back
  on the free list" (only when the remainder leaves room for a
  useful block: `>= header + 1 byte`). Stamps the chosen block's
  `BLOCK_NEXT` with the alloc-magic sentinel. Returns the
  user-data address (block start + 6) or `0` on out-of-memory.
- `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(addr, n)` validates the alloc-magic sentinel
  (catches double-free + invalid-pointer), validates `n` matches
  the recorded block size (catches caller bookkeeping bugs),
  then sorted-inserts into the free list and forward-coalesces
  with the immediate-next free block if their address ranges
  abut.

**Forward coalesce only.** Backward coalesce (merge with the
immediate-previous free block) is deferred. Without it, a
sequence of allocations followed by frees in *forward order*
leaves N separate free blocks; freeing in *reverse order*
chain-coalesces them all. This is fine for SNOBOL4's expected
allocation pattern (LIFO-ish per pattern-match attempt) but
worth revisiting if profiling shows it matters.

## Implementation roadmap

1. **dcpls/`pr/storage-macros`** ✅ — shipped: `include/_plsw_storage.msw`
   with the free-list backend. Reg-rs cases `plsw_storage_basic`,
   `plsw_storage_coalesce`, `plsw_storage_oom`,
   `plsw_storage_double_free`, `plsw_storage_size_mismatch` cover
   the implementation.
2. **dcsno/`pr/storage-allocation-runtime`** — SNOBOL4 builds its
   region/mark/reclaim runtime over PL/SW's primitives.
   See `tools/briefs/dcsno-storage-allocation-runtime.md`.
3. **dcpls/`pr/storage-?macros` (future)** — once PL/SW's macro
   system supports AST-level expansion, add `?GETMAIN` /
   `?FREEMAIN` macros so callers can use the PL/X-style spelling
   instead of the procedure-call form. Procedures stay; macros
   become the preferred surface.
4. **dcpls/`pr/storage-backward-coalesce` (future, only if
   profiled need)** — extend the free-list to coalesce with the
   immediate-previous free block on free, in addition to forward.
5. (Future) Other consumers (Prolog, etc.) layer their policy
   the same way.

## IBM heritage

The `?GETMAIN` / `?FREEMAIN` spelling and the
"`LEN` required on free" semantics come from IBM OS/MVS / OS/390:

```
GETMAIN  RU,LV=DATALEN,A=(R1)
FREEMAIN RU,LV=DATALEN,A=(R1)
```

Both `GETMAIN` and `FREEMAIN` required the length value (`LV=`)
because the OS/360-lineage allocator did not always store size in
an in-band header — it used `GQE`/`FQE` chains stored *outside*
the user region. Callers had to remember the length they
allocated. CICS later relaxed this (CICS tracked allocations
itself).

PL/SW *does* keep an in-band header (`_PLSW_BLOCK_SIZE` is
recorded), so we *could* drop the `LEN` parameter on free. We
keep it for two reasons: (1) PL/X spelling continuity, and
(2) the cross-check between caller-supplied `LEN` and the in-band
size catches a real class of bugs (wrong size remembered, header
corruption).

# Brief: design SNOBOL4's storage runtime over PL/SW primitives

**Owner:** dcsno
**Branch:** `pr/storage-allocation-runtime`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
**Prerequisite:** read
`/disk1/.../work/dcpls/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-plsw/docs/storage-allocation.md`
first. That doc describes the PL/SW substrate this saga builds
on. **This brief is design-and-plan only — the PL/SW
`?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` macros do not exist yet.** Mike will
signal when dcpls's `pr/storage-macros` saga has shipped and
`plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` is available for linking.

You can read this brief now, audit your existing allocation
sites, and draft a runtime design. Don't push the migration
commit until prerequisites are confirmed live.

## Context

SNOBOL4 on PL/SW has a high-frequency allocation pattern:
parsing source, building pattern objects, evaluating matches,
backtracking, building strings. Today the SNOBOL4 source under
`sw-cor24-snobol4/src/` either doesn't allocate (uses static
buffers) or rolls a bump arena ad hoc. As `compiler.sno` and
larger programs land, this stops scaling.

The PL/SW design doc lays out a clean layering:

> PL/SW provides only the raw alloc/free primitives. Region
> boundaries, mark/reclaim, and garbage collection live in the
> consumer's runtime.

That means `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` will give SNOBOL4 a
free-list-backed `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(n), ADDRESS(p), RC(rc))` and
`?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(p), LENGTH(n), RC(rc))`. **Anything beyond
those two primitives — region save/restore, mark/sweep,
generational GC, per-context heaps — is yours.**

Why this split: Prolog wants WAM-style trail unwinding, future
Fortran wants common-block static + stack frames, future C-like
guests want plain malloc/free. Each has its own storage policy
on top of the same dumb substrate. SNOBOL4's policy lives in
SNOBOL4's runtime.

## Goal

After this saga: SNOBOL4 has a documented, implemented storage
runtime that scales to the workloads it'll see (`compiler.sno`,
pattern-heavy demos, etc.). The runtime calls `?GETMAIN` /
`?FREEMAIN` (or the underlying `_PLSW_GETMAIN`/`_PLSW_FREEMAIN`
procedures) as primitives and adds whatever policy SNOBOL4
needs on top.

## Two reasonable designs to choose from

Both are valid. Pick the one that fits SNOBOL4's actual
allocation profile; this brief is not prescriptive about which.

### Design A: GC over a single big region

- One `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(BIG))` at startup carves out the whole
  SNOBOL4 heap (e.g. 32 KB or 64 KB).
- SNOBOL4's runtime owns that region: cell allocator, mark/sweep
  (or copying) GC, root-set traversal of the SNOBOL4 stack /
  variable table, etc. PL/SW's free-list is never touched after
  startup; `?FREEMAIN` is called once at program exit (or never).
- Pros: traditional SNOBOL4 model, no per-cell PL/SW call
  overhead, full control over headers and tags, handles arbitrary
  liveness graphs.
- Cons: more code (a real GC). Need a precise root set, which
  means cooperating with PL/SW's calling convention to find live
  cells in stack frames and registers.

### Design B: region-stack over `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN`

- Multiple `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(REGION_SIZE))` blocks form a stack
  of regions (think arena-per-pattern-match-attempt).
- Each match attempt pushes a region; on backtrack, the region
  is `?FREEMAIN`'d wholesale.
- Long-lived data (symbol table, compiled patterns) lives in a
  base region that's never popped.
- Pros: simpler than full GC; matches SNOBOL4's natural
  pattern-match scope structure; fragmentation is bounded
  because each region is freed wholesale.
- Cons: cells that escape a region (e.g. captured by an outer
  match) need explicit promotion to an older region or
  copy-out. Cells that don't escape are free; cells that do
  cost the copy.

A third hybrid (small fixed-size cell pool for high-churn
allocations, region-stack for variable-size work, GC only over
the symbol table) is also possible. Whichever approach you take,
**the doc-of-record for "what is SNOBOL4's storage model" lives
in `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/`**, not in PL/SW.

## What this saga delivers

Pick one of these scopes; both are reasonable as standalone
sagas:

- **Scope A: Design + plan only.** Audit current allocation
  sites, write `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/storage.md` describing
  the chosen runtime model (A, B, or hybrid), draft an interface
  for the runtime procedures (e.g. `_SNO_ALLOC_CELL`,
  `_SNO_GC_COLLECT`), but don't implement yet. Implementation is
  a follow-up saga.
- **Scope B: Design + minimum runtime.** Same docs as Scope A
  plus an MVP of the chosen runtime — enough to handle
  `examples/hello.sno` and one pattern-matching demo without
  static buffers. Subsequent sagas widen coverage.

Pick whichever fits your bandwidth. If unsure, do Scope A first
— design errors here are cheap to fix on paper, expensive to fix
in shipped runtime code.

## Migration mapping (when ready)

For Scope B (or for whenever the runtime lands), each existing
allocation site moves from `DCL ... BYTE; DCL ... INT INIT(0);`
ad-hoc bump arenas to either:

```pl/i
?GETMAIN(LENGTH(N), ADDRESS(P), RC(RC));
/* ... use P ... */
?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(P), LENGTH(N), RC(RC));
```

… or a SNOBOL4-runtime call that wraps `?GETMAIN` with policy:

```pl/i
P = SNO_ALLOC_CELL(KIND_STRING, length);
/* ... use P ... */
/* GC reclaims when no longer reachable */
```

Inventory your existing call sites with:
```sh
grep -nE 'ARENA_POS|arena_alloc|ALLOC.*PROC' sw-cor24-snobol4/src/
```

## What goes in this PR (Scope A version)

1. Audit of existing allocation sites in `src/`.
2. `docs/storage.md` describing the chosen runtime model.
3. Drafted interface for `_SNO_ALLOC_*` (or whatever names fit)
   procedures.
4. Plan for which allocation sites move first when the runtime
   ships.
5. Optional: a sample `.plsw` showing the call shape, against a
   stub `_PLSW_GETMAIN` that returns 0 (so the design is at
   least syntactically validated against PL/SW today).

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` source — that's dcpls's saga
  (`pr/storage-macros`). Don't implement the substrate; depend
  on it.
- No PL/SW compiler or macro changes.
- No SNOBOL4 language changes (no `.sno` source rewrites).
- No allocation runtime that conflicts with the eventual
  PL/SW substrate (e.g. don't reimplement `?GETMAIN`'s job in
  SNOBOL4 source — call it).

## When done

Push `pr/storage-allocation-runtime` and signal mike. Promotion
to `dev`/`main` is mike's call. After dcpls's `pr/storage-macros`
ships, SNOBOL4's runtime can land in a follow-up saga (or this
saga's Scope B can be extended in place if not yet relayed).

## Questions to answer in your design doc

1. What is the dominant allocation size in SNOBOL4? (Tiny cells?
   Medium strings? Variable patterns?) The answer should drive
   the choice between Design A (GC over big region) and Design B
   (region-stack).
2. What is the rooted set during pattern matching? (i.e. which
   pointers must remain valid across a `?GETMAIN`?) If you can't
   enumerate this concisely, GC is harder; region-stack may be a
   better fit.
3. Are there any natural "scope boundaries" in SNOBOL4 execution
   where you could drop everything cheaply? (Match attempt?
   Statement boundary? Function call?) Region-stack maps cleanly
   onto these.
4. Worst-case live set — how big can the SNOBOL4 heap get before
   you'd consider it pathological? That sets the reasonable
   default for `PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` in your `%INCLUDE plsw_storage`
   line.

# Brief: design SNOBOL4's storage runtime over PL/SW primitives

**Owner:** dcsno
**Branch:** `pr/storage-allocation-runtime`
**Repo:** `sw-cor24-snobol4`
**Prerequisite:** read
`/disk1/.../work/dcpls/github/sw-embed/sw-cor24-plsw/docs/storage-allocation.md`
first. That doc describes the PL/SW substrate this saga builds
on. As of dcpls's `pr/storage-macros`, the substrate is
**shipped**: `include/_plsw_storage.msw` provides
`_PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE)` and `_PLSW_FREEMAIN(USERADDR, LEN)`
procedures over a free-list-backed heap (default 64 KB,
configurable via `%DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE`). Reg-rs cases
`plsw_storage_*` cover alloc, coalesce, OOM, double-free, and
size-mismatch. The PL/X-style `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN` macro
spelling is **deferred** to a future PL/SW saga; callers use
the procedures directly until then.

You can implement against the procedures today.

## Context

SNOBOL4 on PL/SW has a high-frequency allocation pattern:
parsing source, building pattern objects, evaluating matches,
backtracking, building strings. Today the SNOBOL4 source under
`sw-cor24-snobol4/src/` either doesn't allocate (uses static
buffers) or rolls a bump arena ad hoc. As `compiler.sno` and
larger programs land, this stops scaling.

The PL/SW design doc lays out a clean layering:

> PL/SW provides only the raw alloc/free primitives. Region
> boundaries, mark/reclaim, and garbage collection live in the
> consumer's runtime.

That means `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` will give SNOBOL4 a
free-list-backed `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(n), ADDRESS(p), RC(rc))` and
`?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(p), LENGTH(n), RC(rc))`. **Anything beyond
those two primitives — region save/restore, mark/sweep,
generational GC, per-context heaps — is yours.**

Why this split: Prolog wants WAM-style trail unwinding, future
Fortran wants common-block static + stack frames, future C-like
guests want plain malloc/free. Each has its own storage policy
on top of the same dumb substrate. SNOBOL4's policy lives in
SNOBOL4's runtime.

## Goal

After this saga: SNOBOL4 has a documented, implemented storage
runtime that scales to the workloads it'll see (`compiler.sno`,
pattern-heavy demos, etc.). The runtime calls `?GETMAIN` /
`?FREEMAIN` (or the underlying `_PLSW_GETMAIN`/`_PLSW_FREEMAIN`
procedures) as primitives and adds whatever policy SNOBOL4
needs on top.

## Two reasonable designs to choose from

Both are valid. Pick the one that fits SNOBOL4's actual
allocation profile; this brief is not prescriptive about which.

### Design A: GC over a single big region

- One `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(BIG))` at startup carves out the whole
  SNOBOL4 heap (e.g. 32 KB or 64 KB).
- SNOBOL4's runtime owns that region: cell allocator, mark/sweep
  (or copying) GC, root-set traversal of the SNOBOL4 stack /
  variable table, etc. PL/SW's free-list is never touched after
  startup; `?FREEMAIN` is called once at program exit (or never).
- Pros: traditional SNOBOL4 model, no per-cell PL/SW call
  overhead, full control over headers and tags, handles arbitrary
  liveness graphs.
- Cons: more code (a real GC). Need a precise root set, which
  means cooperating with PL/SW's calling convention to find live
  cells in stack frames and registers.

### Design B: region-stack over `?GETMAIN`/`?FREEMAIN`

- Multiple `?GETMAIN(LENGTH(REGION_SIZE))` blocks form a stack
  of regions (think arena-per-pattern-match-attempt).
- Each match attempt pushes a region; on backtrack, the region
  is `?FREEMAIN`'d wholesale.
- Long-lived data (symbol table, compiled patterns) lives in a
  base region that's never popped.
- Pros: simpler than full GC; matches SNOBOL4's natural
  pattern-match scope structure; fragmentation is bounded
  because each region is freed wholesale.
- Cons: cells that escape a region (e.g. captured by an outer
  match) need explicit promotion to an older region or
  copy-out. Cells that don't escape are free; cells that do
  cost the copy.

A third hybrid (small fixed-size cell pool for high-churn
allocations, region-stack for variable-size work, GC only over
the symbol table) is also possible. Whichever approach you take,
**the doc-of-record for "what is SNOBOL4's storage model" lives
in `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/`**, not in PL/SW.

## What this saga delivers

Pick one of these scopes; both are reasonable as standalone
sagas:

- **Scope A: Design + plan only.** Audit current allocation
  sites, write `sw-cor24-snobol4/docs/storage.md` describing
  the chosen runtime model (A, B, or hybrid), draft an interface
  for the runtime procedures (e.g. `_SNO_ALLOC_CELL`,
  `_SNO_GC_COLLECT`), but don't implement yet. Implementation is
  a follow-up saga.
- **Scope B: Design + minimum runtime.** Same docs as Scope A
  plus an MVP of the chosen runtime — enough to handle
  `examples/hello.sno` and one pattern-matching demo without
  static buffers. Subsequent sagas widen coverage.

Pick whichever fits your bandwidth. If unsure, do Scope A first
— design errors here are cheap to fix on paper, expensive to fix
in shipped runtime code.

## Migration mapping (when ready)

For Scope B (or for whenever the runtime lands), each existing
allocation site moves from `DCL ... BYTE; DCL ... INT INIT(0);`
ad-hoc bump arenas to either:

```pl/i
?GETMAIN(LENGTH(N), ADDRESS(P), RC(RC));
/* ... use P ... */
?FREEMAIN(ADDRESS(P), LENGTH(N), RC(RC));
```

… or a SNOBOL4-runtime call that wraps `?GETMAIN` with policy:

```pl/i
P = SNO_ALLOC_CELL(KIND_STRING, length);
/* ... use P ... */
/* GC reclaims when no longer reachable */
```

Inventory your existing call sites with:
```sh
grep -nE 'ARENA_POS|arena_alloc|ALLOC.*PROC' sw-cor24-snobol4/src/
```

## What goes in this PR (Scope A version)

1. Audit of existing allocation sites in `src/`.
2. `docs/storage.md` describing the chosen runtime model.
3. Drafted interface for `_SNO_ALLOC_*` (or whatever names fit)
   procedures.
4. Plan for which allocation sites move first when the runtime
   ships.
5. Optional: a sample `.plsw` showing the call shape, against a
   stub `_PLSW_GETMAIN` that returns 0 (so the design is at
   least syntactically validated against PL/SW today).

## What does NOT go in this PR

- No `plsw_storage.{msw,plsw}` source — that's dcpls's saga
  (`pr/storage-macros`). Don't implement the substrate; depend
  on it.
- No PL/SW compiler or macro changes.
- No SNOBOL4 language changes (no `.sno` source rewrites).
- No allocation runtime that conflicts with the eventual
  PL/SW substrate (e.g. don't reimplement `?GETMAIN`'s job in
  SNOBOL4 source — call it).

## When done

Push `pr/storage-allocation-runtime` and signal mike. Promotion
to `dev`/`main` is mike's call. After dcpls's `pr/storage-macros`
ships, SNOBOL4's runtime can land in a follow-up saga (or this
saga's Scope B can be extended in place if not yet relayed).

## Questions to answer in your design doc

1. What is the dominant allocation size in SNOBOL4? (Tiny cells?
   Medium strings? Variable patterns?) The answer should drive
   the choice between Design A (GC over big region) and Design B
   (region-stack).
2. What is the rooted set during pattern matching? (i.e. which
   pointers must remain valid across a `?GETMAIN`?) If you can't
   enumerate this concisely, GC is harder; region-stack may be a
   better fit.
3. Are there any natural "scope boundaries" in SNOBOL4 execution
   where you could drop everything cheaply? (Match attempt?
   Statement boundary? Function call?) Region-stack maps cleanly
   onto these.
4. Worst-case live set — how big can the SNOBOL4 heap get before
   you'd consider it pathological? That sets the reasonable
   default for `PLSW_HEAP_SIZE` in your `%INCLUDE plsw_storage`
   line.

git add -A && git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
feat(storage): _PLSW_GETMAIN/_PLSW_FREEMAIN free-list allocator

Implements the substrate from docs/storage-allocation.md as a
single inline include/_plsw_storage.msw. The PL/X-style
?GETMAIN/?FREEMAIN macro spelling is deferred (PL/SW's MACRODEF/
GEN system emits assembly only and can't synthesize the right
code for runtime-variable LENGTH or stack-frame-local ADDRESS);
callers use the procedures directly until that capability lands.

include/_plsw_storage.msw
- %DEFINE PLSW_HEAP_SIZE (default 65536) sets the heap size;
  override with %DEFINE before %INCLUDE.
- _PLSW_BLOCK BASED template: 6-byte header (3-byte BLOCK_SIZE
  + 3-byte BLOCK_NEXT). BLOCK_NEXT = next-free-addr when free,
  or 0xFFFFFF (alloc-magic sentinel) when allocated.
- Lazy init on first _PLSW_GETMAIN: one giant free block.
- _PLSW_GETMAIN(SIZE) -> user address or 0 on OOM. First-fit;
  splits when remainder leaves room for >=7 bytes; stamps the
  alloc-magic on the chosen block.
- _PLSW_FREEMAIN(USERADDR, LEN) -> 0/1/2:
    0 = success; sorted-insert into free list, forward-coalesce
        with immediate-next free block when ranges abut.
    1 = double-free / invalid pointer (alloc-magic not present).
    2 = size mismatch (LEN doesn't match recorded BLOCK_SIZE).
- PLSW_STORAGE_HEADERS_ONLY guard: non-entry modules skip impl
  + heap declarations (multi-module builds keep one canonical
  heap in the entry module).

Demos (examples/storage_*.plsw, all reg-rs goldens):
- storage_basic: alloc 12, free 12, both succeed.
- storage_coalesce: alloc 3x100, free in reverse, alloc 800
  succeeds (forward coalesce reconstitutes the heap).
- storage_oom: alloc 1024 against 256-byte heap returns 0;
  subsequent in-bounds alloc still succeeds (allocator stays
  in valid state after OOM).
- storage_double_free: first free returns 0, second returns 1
  (alloc-magic detection).
- storage_size_mismatch: free with wrong LEN returns 2; correct
  LEN afterwards still works.

tests/driver.sh + scripts/bootstrap-goldens.sh wired with the
five new cases. just test now passes 15/15.

docs/storage-allocation.md
- Status: v1 implemented (procedures shipped; macros deferred).
- Procedure contract: signatures, return-code semantics, the
  deliberate decision to require LEN on free per IBM heritage
  (cross-checks against in-band header to catch bookkeeping bugs).
- Rewrote opt-in pattern from two-file to single-file inline,
  plus a "Why single-file" note covering the trade-off vs the
  modular .msw + .plsw form (still a viable future direction).
- Implementation roadmap updated: pr/storage-macros = ✅;
  pr/storage-?macros (future, gated on PL/SW macro AST-level
  expansion); pr/storage-backward-coalesce (future, profiled).
- IBM heritage section explains the LEN-on-free decision with
  reference to GETMAIN RU,LV=DATALEN syntax.

tools/briefs/dcsno-storage-allocation-runtime.md (agent-drafted)
- Updated to reflect that the substrate has shipped: dcsno can
  implement against the procedures today rather than waiting on
  prereqs. Macro spelling deferred but procedure layer is real.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
